newsitem.title: MALTA: FEATURE - Treasure trove of aircraft wrecks found off Malta.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Treasure trove of aircraft wrecks found off Malta.

text.p: Italian minesweepers using sophisticated underwater search equipment have found a treasure trove of aircraft wrecks in Maltese waters, and aviation enthusiasts hope some can be recovered for a museum.
For although Malta has an 80-year aviation history, not one old plane has survived for public display on the island in the middle of the Mediterranean.
Some of the world's early aviators stopped in Malta to refuel during their record-breaking flights.

Malta was also the scene of some of the fiercest aerial fighting of World War Two as German and Italian aircraft based in Sicily 60 miles (100 km) to the north bombed its airfields day and night to deny air cover to the allies along the Mediterranean sea lanes.
Hundreds of aircraft ended up in the sea. Most were shot down and many others were dumped there by the British after they became surplus as hostilities ended.

All that survived were the skeletal remains of the fuselage of a Sea Gladiator, one of a trio of biplanes nicknamed Faith, Hope and Charity -- Malta's only air defence against the modern Italian air force in the first weeks of the war.
That fuselage was presented to the Maltese people by the British Royal Air Force in 1943 after it was recovered from a stone quarry where it had been dumped.
It gained a place in Malta's "armoury" alongside swords and suits of armour left by the Knights of St. John 400 years before.
Interest in setting up an air museum took root when a bank official, Ray Polidano, spotted the wreckage of a Spitfire fuselage in a field several years ago.

British aircraft restorers had been there before him and decided it was useless, but Polidano teamed up with several volunteers including army Lieutenant Mark Said and persuaded his employer, Mid-Med Bank, to back the project.
"Before that, I had only built plastic model aircraft," Polidano told Reuters.

"By a stroke of luck, an elderly British aircraft restoration expert happened to be in Malta. I showed him the Spitfire and he decided there and then he would stay in Malta for a month and show us how to prepare the Spitfire for static display," he said.
The work took years to complete, but it was the team's inexperience rather than spare parts that was the problem.

"Instead of sending for spare parts from abroad, we got them from the bottom of the sea. We have a storehouse of parts on the seabed and whenever we needed anything, we just went down and got it," Said recalled.
The Spitfire, restored although not in flying condition, was rolled out for Malta's VE Day celebrations last year and a Malta Aviation Foundation was created to set up an aviation museum.
Polidano has started work on restoring a wartime British Hurricane fighter, also recovered from the sea.
"Most aircraft parts keep rather well in the sea. The problem is the aluminium and magnesium parts, which deteriorate rather quickly," he said.
Wreckage is usually encrusted if found in shallow water. It is in better condition in the deep, when it is also harder to recover.
Polidano said his team tries to rebuild the wreckage of one aircraft rather than assemble a "new" plane from several parts.
"We try to restore the remains of an aircraft after we have identified it and researched its history.

"Two years ago we recovered parts of a Seafire (the naval version of a Spitfire). Research on the aircraft at the Fleet Air Arm Museum showed it was dumped in 1945 from a British aircraft carrier, HMS Attacker, after another aircraft landed on top of it.
"We even found that its last pilot was still alive, and he was immensely interested in the remains of his aircraft," Polidano said.

Since it was set up last year, the Malta Aviation Foundation has bought a wartime Dakota transport aircraft and been promised a De Havilland Vampire, one of the earliest jets in the British fleet air arm.
Said recalled that bad weather hampered the first search in September by Italian minesweepers but although only a few miles (kms) were covered, the results could not have been more encouraging.
"Over a two-mile (three km) stretch we found about 20 wrecks. However there are hundreds of other remains which still have to be located," he said.
Among the wrecks were a wartime RAF Wellington bomber, an Italian fighter and a post-war Fleet Air Arm Sea Fury, all in excellent condition.
Their location is being kept secret to prevent theft, although Said added that the depth would make recovery difficult unless specialised equipment was used.
In all cases there was no sign of crew members' remains. "We cannot touch aircraft if there are human remains in them. They are considered war graves," Said stressed.
Italian Navy Captain Angelino Tommaso, deputy director of public information, praised the crews of the minesweepers.
"We have done good work in recovering part of Malta's history and we hope to come again next year to finish off what the bad weather prevented us from doing."
